newsitem.title: USA: Oil price impact on US inflation, Fed seen marginal.
newsitem.headline: Oil price impact on US inflation, Fed seen marginal.

text.p: A spike in oil prices following the launch of a U.S. air strike against Iraq could have a marginally negative impact on an otherwise benign U.S. inflation picture if it persists, economists said on Tuesday.

But while higher energy prices would likely factor into the thinking of Federal Reserve policymakers, wage inflation and overall growth prospects are currently the decisive policy-formulating criteria for the central bank, they noted.
As a result, the oil price jump -- which was showing signs of fading by early afternoon -- promises to be only one small piece of a larger inflation puzzle for the Fed.
"A rise in oil prices does play some role, but the Fed's stress has been on core inflation," which excludes food and energy prices, said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co Inc.
"And the overall inflation focus for the Fed has been on pressures in the labor market and the overall speed of the economy," he added.

Oil prices surged by as much as $2.00 in early trade after market players returned from a long Labor Day weekend to news of U.S. military action against Iraq. The attack came in response to Baghdad's incursion into protected Kurdish zones in the north of Iraq.
The Iraqi attack led to an over-the-weekend suspension of a deal that would have allowed Iraq to sell up to $2.0 billion in oil over the next six months.
By early afternoon, however, profit-taking had knocked oil prices off their highs. At 1300 EDT/1700 GMT, October NYMEX crude oil was up $0.88 per barrel at $23.13.

Economists noted that even before the latest Iraq news, oil prices had risen over $3.00 per barrel since mid-June. The latest jump could aggravate overall inflation numbers in the coming months, but not overly so.

"During the first seven months of the year inflation was running at a 3.5-percent rate," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc. "What these events could do is boost the numbers into the upper 3.0-percent range, but I don't think we're necessarily headed for a major increase in inflation from this."
Oil analysts said that when the dust has settled, the suspension of the Iraqi oil deal was likely to add about $1.50 per barrel to the price of crude.
However, until evidence of a sustained price move emerges, economists warned against drawing any new conclusions about the consumer price outlook.
"What we've seen is a reflexive reaction to the political and military developments," said Ed McKelvey, senior economist at Goldman, Sachs & Co.

"The key is how persistent it will be. Only if you get a pronounced and sustained upward move could we talk about an impact (on consumer inflation), and right now it's very premature to think about that."
